client: I've been really stressed out this past week because I have this big presentation at an annual conference coming up, and after I completely blanked during practice yesterday, I just... I don't know, it feels like everything is falling apart. My mind keeps replaying that moment over and over, and I can't stop thinking about how humiliating it's going to be if that happens in front of hundreds of people. I'm honestly not sure talking about it is going to make the anxiety go away, but I figured I'd give it a shot.
therapist: Thank you for giving this a shot — even that small step takes courage, especially when you're already carrying so much. I can hear in your voice a kind of quiet exhaustion beneath the worry, like you're holding a lot of tension inward, and it makes sense that your mind keeps replaying that moment — that's actually a very common anxiety response, not a sign that things are truly "falling apart." One thing we can gently explore together is whether that one practice stumble is solid *evidence* that you'll blank at the real presentation, or whether your mind might be treating a fear as a certainty.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I appreciate it, but honestly it's hard to just tell myself "it's only one stumble" when it felt so total, like my mind just went completely blank for what felt like forever. I've done presentations before and been nervous, but this was different — I couldn't even remember the opening line I'd practiced a hundred times. So part of me wonders if exploring whether it's "evidence" or not is really going to change how terrified I feel when I'm actually standing up there.
therapist: That's a really important pushback, and you're right that reframing alone doesn't make the fear in your body disappear — and I notice you're speaking quickly and softly, like the anxiety is right there even as we talk. What you're describing, that total blankness, often happens when our nervous system goes into overdrive and actually *interferes* with memory retrieval — it wasn't a sign your knowledge was gone, it was your anxiety doing exactly what anxiety does. So rather than just challenging the thought, we might also work on helping your nervous system feel safer in that moment, so your mind has room to access what you already know.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Okay, that actually makes some sense to me — the idea that my brain wasn't broken, it was just flooded. But I guess my worry is, how do I make my nervous system "feel safer" when the whole situation is genuinely high-stakes and scary? Like, I can't just pretend the stakes aren't real, and I'm not sure breathing exercises or whatever are going to cut it when I'm standing in front of hundreds of people who are judging every word I say.
therapist: You're absolutely right that the stakes *are* real, and I don't want to hand you something that feels like a band-aid — I can hear that you're wound pretty tight right now even just talking through this, which tells me how much this matters to you. The goal isn't to pretend the pressure away, but to shift your relationship with it — research actually shows that reframing anxiety as *excitement* ("I'm activated because this matters") rather than threat can meaningfully improve performance, because your body's response is nearly identical, but your mind stops fighting it. We can also work on building a reliable "anchor" — something concrete and practiced enough that even a flooded brain can find it — so you have a real tool, not just a breathing cue, to return to when the moment gets intense.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The excitement reframe is interesting, and I've actually heard that before somewhere, but when I try to apply it in the moment it just feels... fake, like I'm lying to myself, because my body knows it's scared not excited. I'm also not sure what you mean by an "anchor" exactly — like, is that something I'd actually be able to access when my mind goes completely blank, or is it more of a thing that works in theory but falls apart under real pressure? I guess I'm just worried about investing in another strategy that sounds good right now but lets me down when it actually counts.
therapist: Your skepticism is actually really healthy here, and I notice even as you're questioning these ideas, there's an energy in your voice that sounds less like defeat and more like someone who genuinely wants something that *works* — which is something we can build on. An anchor isn't a mantra you repeat to yourself; it's something physical and automatic, like pressing your feet firmly into the floor or pausing to find one specific point of focus, practiced so many times beforehand that your body can do it even when your mind is blank. And you're right to hold strategies accountable — so rather than taking my word for it, what if we actually tested a small version of this together, so you can judge for yourself whether it's real or just theory?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, testing it out here feels less intimidating than just trusting it blindly, so I'm willing to try that. But I want to be honest — even if it works right now in this room, I'm not sure it'll translate to being on a stage with a microphone and a crowd staring at me, because this feels like a completely different kind of pressure. I guess I'm just scared of building up hope in something and then having it collapse at the worst possible moment.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, pitched high, like you're bracing for disappointment even as you're opening the door — tells me this fear of hope collapsing might actually be harder than the presentation fear itself. That's a really vulnerable thing to name, and it matters. What you're describing is something we can work with directly in CBT: the belief that "if I invest and it fails, that's worse than not trying" — and it's worth gently asking whether protecting yourself from hope has actually been keeping you safe, or whether it's been its own kind of cost.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me, because honestly... yeah, I think protecting myself from hope has become its own habit, and I'm not sure it's actually made me feel safer — it's just made everything feel more exhausting and kind of lonely. But it's hard to just decide to let that guard down, because every time I've gotten my hopes up about something and it didn't work out, the crash felt so much worse than if I hadn't tried at all. I don't know how you change something that feels that deeply wired in.
therapist: The way you just said that — your voice carrying something that sounds like a quiet ache, like you've been holding this for a long time — tells me this goes much deeper than presentation anxiety, and I want to honor how significant that recognition is. You're not broken or "wired wrong"; what you're describing is a completely logical protection strategy that your mind built after real experiences of disappointment, and it made sense when it was formed. The work isn't about forcing yourself to suddenly trust hope, but slowly and carefully gathering new evidence — starting small enough that the risk feels manageable — so your nervous system can learn that reaching for something doesn't always end in freefall.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That framing — that it was a logical protection strategy, not some flaw in me — actually lands differently than I expected, and I notice I feel a little less like I'm fighting myself when I hear it that way. But "gathering new evidence slowly" sounds like it could take a really long time, and I have this presentation in less than two weeks, so I'm worried we're getting into territory that feels important but maybe not immediately useful for what's right in front of me. I guess I'm wondering how we bring this back to something concrete I can actually use before I walk out onto that stage.
therapist: I can hear a real shift in you just now — there's an urgency and aliveness in your voice that feels less like panic and more like someone who's ready to move forward, which is exactly the right energy for what's ahead. So let's make this concrete: the most powerful thing you can do in the next two weeks isn't memorizing more content, it's deliberately practicing under mild pressure — running through your opening in front of even one or two people, using your physical anchor, so your nervous system builds a memory of *surviving* the discomfort rather than only knowing the blank-out moment. That way, when you walk onto that stage, your brain has recent, real evidence that it can handle the flood — not just a hope that it might.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually makes sense to me in a way that feels doable rather than overwhelming, and I think I could ask my roommate to sit through my opening section once or twice this week. But I'm already anticipating the awkwardness of asking someone to do that — like, what if I blank in front of them too, and then I've just added another humiliating moment to the mental replay reel instead of a good memory? I guess I'm wondering if there's a way to set it up so that even if it goes badly, it still counts as useful rather than just more evidence against me.
therapist: I notice something important in how you just framed that — you're already thinking ahead, trying to protect the experiment from becoming more ammunition against yourself, which is actually a really sophisticated instinct. The key is going in with a explicit agreement with yourself beforehand: *any* attempt counts as a success, because the goal isn't a perfect run-through, it's exposing your nervous system to the discomfort and proving it doesn't destroy you — so a blank moment in front of your roommate becomes data that you survived it, not evidence of failure. If you can define "useful" before you start rather than judging it after, you take away the reel's power to rewrite what actually happened.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I really like the idea of deciding what "success" means before I start, because you're right that I usually only judge how things went after the fact, and by then my anxiety has already spun the story. But I'm honestly not sure I'll be able to hold onto that agreement in the moment — like, I can nod along to it now, but when I'm actually standing there freezing in front of my roommate, I'm worried the old instinct to just label it a disaster will kick in automatically. Is there something more concrete I can do to actually lock that definition in, rather than just hoping I'll remember it when things get hard?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, pitched high, like your mind is already racing ahead to the moment it might go wrong — actually proves exactly why we need something external rather than just an internal promise. So here's something concrete: write your definition of success on a small card *before* the practice, something like "I showed up and let myself be seen," and physically hand it to your roommate to read back to you afterward — that way the anchor exists outside your anxious mind and can't be rewritten by it in the moment. It turns your roommate from just an audience into an actual partner in the experiment, and gives the agreement a real form that your anxiety can't quietly erase.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's actually a really concrete idea, and I like that it takes the judgment out of my own hands in that moment because I clearly can't trust myself to be fair about it. But I'm a little worried about how my roommate will react — like, asking them to read a card back to me feels kind of vulnerable and maybe even weird, and I don't want them to think I'm falling apart over a work presentation. I guess I'm wondering if there's a way to explain it to them without it feeling like I'm making a bigger deal out of this than it already is.
therapist: There's something tender in how you're speaking right now — even as you're making real progress, there's a quiet worry about being seen as "too much," which tells me the vulnerability here isn't just about the presentation but about letting someone close to you see that you're struggling. Here's a reframe: you don't have to present it as falling apart — you could simply tell your roommate "I'm working on a technique to manage performance nerves and I need a practice partner," which is completely true, genuinely interesting, and asks for their help without requiring you to expose more than you're ready to. Most people feel *honored* to be asked for that kind of specific, purposeful support — it's not a burden, it's an invitation to matter to you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
